SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview of
Hayes Pillars
Tapes 1, 2, 3
Interview by Samuel Floyd

St. Louis, Missouri
March 2, 1977

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS

Interview with Mr. Hayes Pillars, March 2nd, 1977, St. Louis, Missouri. Mr. Pillars, can you begin please by telling us something about your parents, your boyhood, when you were born, that kind of thing?

Yes. I was born in North Little Rock, Arkansas. The town was called Argenta, Arkansas at the time of birth and in later years it was -- the name was changed to North Little Rock, Arkansas. April the 30th, 1906. I lived at 311 North 21st Street in North Little Rock.

I can remember far back when I was three years old when my brother Charles was born, because my mother -- my aunt told me to go down on the next block and play with the kids. And I noticed they were quite liberal about asking me to go and play. And when I came back later on that afternoon, I had a new brother, Charles Pillars. And I'm three years older than he.

And at the age of six I can remember my mother and father would take me out to see various shows that would come through town, like the circus, and carnivals and things like that. My father would put me on his shoulder, and we would walk around. And before I go into that, I'd like to tell you about my father.
At that time my father worked for the Vestle Floral Company in North Little Rock, and he drove a team of horses and
delivered flowers to the various fellows in North Little Rock and Little Rock, Arkansas.

He took a great interest in me because in the evenings when he would come home, he would dress me up and put me in the horse and buggy, and we would drive out to see friends and drive by to see friends of the family. And he'd always tell me that when I got in front of different friends' home to watch him and tip my hat like he would tip his hat. And he taught me to be polite to people, speak to them, and tip my hat to ladies and older people. This I never forgot.

My father worked on this job a few years, and something happened on the job and he quit the job. And we had a rough going there for a while. So, finally my father was hired as a janitor at the Post Office. And I can remember him saying the salary was $500.00 a year. And when payday would come, my father would have to wait sometimes four, and five, and six, and sometimes a week and a half or two weeks before he would get his check. That's the way the government operated back in those days. And that worked a hardship on my mother, trying to stay within the budget of my father's income.

We came up in the early years seeming that we had plenty of food to eat, and my father bought us plenty of clothes and things like that. And then the third boy came along. My brother Herbert came along. And in the meantime things began to get a little tough for us.

Before I go into that phase of my early life, I would like to mention the fact that when I was six or seven years old at one of those shows, I can remember it was a big circus. And they had a big brass band, and a big wagon drawn by horses. And the band was playing, and the elephants were marching. You know, you could see the wild animals in the cages of the wagons.

And on the end of the parade was a black band in a great big truck playing "The Memphis Blues." And I thought that was one of the most beautiful songs I had ever heard. "The Memphis Blues." From that time on it seems like music to me was magic. And every time there was a show in town, my father would always take me.
And as time went on another song came upon the horizon, "The St. Louis Blues." And I just fell in love with the "St. Louis Blues." It just seemed that the music was in my bones, and I just loved it.

My father in the meantime was a drill master. He belonged to a lodge called "The Tabernacle Lodge," and they featured at their yearly convention different troops of boys and women drilling, and the best team would always win a prize. So, my father put me in the drill corps, and the type of drilling was in rhythm. It was your left foot was always the odd number, and your right foot was always the even number. Like one, two, left, right, left, right. Left one, right two.

And all the kids that drilled with him had to have that rhythm or that sense of rhythm in order to belong to the drill corps. And in drilling we would make different letters like the letter A, the letter B, the letter C, and we would do it in uniform. And every summer we would go from -- to various cities in the state of Arkansas.

And I can remember the first city that we visited was Forest City, Arkansas. And I remember there were no paved streets. All the streets were dusty and dirt. And they had a brass band there playing. And the brass band was playing a song named "Dar-dane-lla." And I thought that was the prettiest band, the prettiest song -- one of the prettiest songs I'd ever heard. And I just hung around that band every day that the band played. Of course, it was about for three days we were there.
And each year we would do to various cities, like Hot Springs one year, Pine Bluff another year, sometimes back to Little Rock one year, then back to Hot Springs, and on and on.

As I grew a little older, things got a little rougher for the family and I would go out and seek jobs. And I can remember back in 1918 -- back in 1917 rather -- was a real cold winter. And most kids would -- young boy -- young kids would hop freight trains, jump up on the coal cars and throw off coal, and put that coal in a crocus sack and put it on our shoulders,
and haul that coal home so that we could have heat for the wintertime. That was in 1917.

I can remember in 1918 -- the summer of 1918 I got a job.-- it was during the war -- driving a team of mules. And back in those days they had what they called wheelers, a two wheel -- two wheels with a big shovel on it. And you had to get up early in the morning to go to the corral and put the collar and put the harness on your horse -- I mean on your mule. And I was too young to catch my mule, and the fellows would curse me out but they would help me put the harness on my mules.

And my salary during that time was three and a half a day, which was a lot of money. But I was trying to bring money into the family to help my father feed us all. And that job lasted through the summer. And, of course, later on in November of 1919, I think it was, was when the Armistice was signed.

I was going to high school then. The Armistice was signed in 1919, if I'm correct. I think it was 1919. And I was going to high school in North Little Rock. They called it the North Little Rock Colored High School. And I heard -- in 1920 I heard about a high school in Little Rock, Arkansas where they had a band -- the school had a band, and I got the impression that if you went to that school and you wanted to play in the band they would buy you an instrument.
So, I knew some friends who had moved to Little Rock
in the 3200 block on Main Street, and I asked them could I use their address because I wanted to change schools. And they said yes.

I changed school and went to Gibbs High School for one semester. But I found out that if you wanted to be in the band you had to have your own instrument. And I admired the various ones who were playing the band in the band. And I just said to myself, 'One of these days I just hope I'll be able to buy an instrument and play in the band.'

I went to high school there for that semester, and then I came on back over to my home town and went back to my regular school. And shortly after that things got so rough in my home town until they started charging tuition to go to high school. I just forget how much the tuition was. I think it was $1.50 or $2.00 a month, or something like that.

A boy named Walter Baker and myself applied for the job of making fires in the stoves in the school in order to keep from paying the tuition. This was the only way I could go to school, because my father wasn't able to support me.

So, we got the job. This school building had eight rooms; four down and four up. Walter Baker made the fires on one side, and I made the fires on the other. And we did that for about a semester, a semester and a half. Things were getting rough. I got me a job shining shoes. I worked at that for a while, and got me a job -- water boy on the boiler job. I worked at that

for a while. I got a job at a piano company wiping off pianos and keeping the place clean, and I got fired off that job because as soon as I would clean up the front windows and the front, and wipe off the pianos, I would go up on the fifth floor and play a piano. So, the boss caught me up there playing the player piano, and he fired me. I was making three and a half a week at the time that I got fired.

So, as times went on, my father had changed jobs. And he worked -- got a job at the Missouri Pacific Shop. And I was getting to be a pretty big boy. I was approaching 16 years of age. And the superintendent of the shop saw my father one day with a pair of my trousers on, and he asked my father whose trousers were they. And he told him that they were his son's trousers. He said, 'Well, by God, bring him down here and we'll give him a job.

So, I went down that summer, the summer of 1922, and he gave me a job working in the machine shop cleaning up. In the meantime I had my mind set on playing music. But before I go into that -- before I go into 1920, let me tell you what happened a year or two before that.

We were evicted from our house where we lived on 21st Street, and we had to move into -- we moved from a four room house into a three room house at 423 West 24th Street. And the house was right on the corner, and it was right on the sidewalk. And you could be inside the window and you could hear
people as they passed this house. And this made me rather ashamed to have to move from the nice home that I thought we had to this particular place at 423 West 24th Street.
It was a three room shotgun type house, frame building. And when it rained at nights or in the daytime, you had to get tin cans and put things around to catch the rain.

Well, I took this job in 1920 with my father, working on this job as a laborer. And I said to myself, the first thing I was going to do, I was going to help my father pay for that piece of property and build a new house on it. So, my father and I got together, and as we got paid we would take every penny and put that money up, and put it on a building fund.

And by 1963 -- I mean 1923 we had finished paying for the house, and we had enough money to pay down -- to have carpenters come in and to move that house a little bit away from the street and add two more rooms to it. And I sacrificed every penny that I made to do this.

In the meantime I was falling in love -- had fallen in love with music. Come April in 1923, I told my dad I wanted to buy a saxophone. My dad says, "Well, if you want to buy a saxophone, Hayes, then go ahead. It's pretty expensive but if you think you can make it, go ahead. I'll help you." I went to a gentleman named Art -- Mr. Art Beam. Mr. Art Beam was a musician, and he sold instruments. And I had to go to see my horn and go on the back porch. He didn't invite me into his
house. I had to go in the back of the back porch to see this horn.

And I can remember it was a Holten horn. It wasn't exactly new, but it looked like new. And he charged me $151.60 for that horn. I gave him a down payment of $50.00. And my father stood for the horn and told him we would pay for it in a few months.

And in the meantime he asked me to come inside in order to sign some papers. This I did. While inside he was teaching some of the white kids how to play the saxophone, and I noticed the kids running the scale over the saxophone, as they would start at the low key C and run up to middle C on the horn. I didn't know what C was. I called that 'doe.' Doe, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, doe. Because I had been taught that in high school. I didn't know the difference between instrumental music and vocal music.
How old were you at this time?
I was 16 years old.
What did the --
I was 17 years old. 17 years old. Let's see. Let's see. I was 17 years old.
And the music you studied in school, was this music theory hearing or --
The music I studied in school was regular -- just regular vocal music, you know, the teachers
would teach you, you know, in grammar school. You know, do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do.
I see.
Do, ti, la, so, fa, mi, re, do. They taught us that, see. And we would sing songs, you know what I mean.
Yeah.

And I used to sing in the Glee Club in high school. And then they had me singing with a group of girls, and they put me right in the middle. And at that time I was supposed to have had a pretty nice voice. And my music teacher, Mrs. Hewey, would always -- was always telling me, "Well, Hayes, I'm going to make you learn because you have it in you." You know how kids would play a lot, you know. But she would tell me, "I'm going to make you learn this, Hayes, because you have it in you." One of those kind of things.
So, I knew a little about vocal music. A little bit, you know, man.
I see.

So, as they -- as the saxophone -- I noticed the guys, they were -- these three fingers would be down -- and these three fingers would be down, and this right finger would be down and that would be do. And as they would raise the finger up, do re -- as they raised the finger up, it was just a different note, you know, up -- going up. Always up. Then
when they would get to the top note, it would -- to hit C would use that center finger to C. And I stood there and I watched that. I watched that and I watched that.

When I took that home -- when I picked that horn up and took it home, the first thing I did was take my chart out and put it across the bed, and took my horn out and just started blowing and blowing. And I just went down -- and my fingers -- I just CALLED myself figuring the fingers out. And I kept on blowing and blowing. I finally got this low note out, and I -- da da -- kept on running. And before I went to bed I was running the scale. But I thought it was do, re, me, fa, so, la, ti, do. That's what I thought, see.
Had you ever played the saxophone at all before?
Had never played the saxophone at all before.
How did you solve the embouchure problem?

I didn't solve it. I just started blowing. And I started blowing wrong, and I still -- I'll be blowing that way the rest of my life. My embouchure, I just started blowing. This was force, just sheer force. Then after I had played my horn about a year, I found out you should put your teeth over your horn and grip the mouthpiece with your teeth. You know what I mean. And you form an embouchure like that.

Well, everybody claimed I sounded so good the way I was playing, why change. And I noticed one day I tried to put my teeth on there, and it jarred me. It just shook my head, you know, man. And I said, 'Well, I'm just going to stick to my way of blowing my horn.' Then I found out in later years that most saxophone players who had blown that way -- the orthodox way of playing a saxophone -- their teeth -- they had worked a little curve in their teeth. A little curve in their teeth.

Just like my partner Jater-- (unintelligible) his teeth finally wore out and he had to have new teeth put in up there. And I still got my two front teeth, because I never used them that way, you know.

And -- but this is what I did. I pulled the chart out. And I looked on the chart and I didn't see a thing about do or anything like that. (Interruption) Ready? I noticed when I got home that night, as I said before, I kept fooling with my horn, blowing, blowing, blowing, until I was able to run the C scale. It sound terrible, but it sound good to me.

The next day I found out that there was a big difference between vocal music and instrumental music. Instrumental music, you work by C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C, and the vocal is do, re, me, fa, so, la, ti, do. So, then I had to learn the C, D -- I had to learn the spaces and the lines, you know, what they were, see.

And so, I bent myself in that book every morning and every night. The people in the community were mad with me, and they called me everything but child of God. (unintelligible). Even my father got sick of me around the house. And my mother would tell my dad, 'Leave him alone. Leave him alone.'

And I sacrificed everything, all of my pleasures that a youngster would have, in order to try and learn that horn, because the man had told me that he couldn't teach me because I was colored. Mr. Beam told me that he couldn't teach me because I was colored -- after I had bought the horn from him.

I studied and studied and studied. I joined a little group, a band, a bunch of older fellows down -- who lived down from me downtown. And I used to go to rehearsals. And I'd sit up there and have the music out. I didn't know what I was doing, but I was in the band and I was trying. And they weren't much better. But we all were trying to be musicians.

And I can remember I had a little music lyre that fitted on my saxophone. And I'd put this little band music up there, and I'd look at it, and I'd look at it, and I'd look at it, and I'd look at it. So, finally I just kept blowing and blowing and blowing, and taking pieces (inaudible) of my instructor. And I would take it just bar -- I would spend sometimes a whole day on one bar. And I just counted out -- I beats would just count it out, like four piece to a bar. Four piece

you divide that between a four. And if you want to double it up, it'd be eight. And if you wanted to double that it, it'd be 16. And you were just playing arithmetic. And I just used that, and I would take -- I would just work at one bar at a time.
And I'd work and work and work, and I got so that I could see the light.
When you use the word "instructor" you're talking about the text --
Textbook.
-- the book?
Yeah, the book. This book.
The instruction book.
This instruction book. That's what I mean, an instruction book. An instruction book.
Were you getting any help from any of your --
No.
-- band members?

That was because they couldn't play saxophone at all. They couldn't play saxophone, and they didn't know as much about it as I did. But what happened, there was -- I found there was a white teacher that taught saxophone and lived in Little Rock. I contacted him. I went to him and took one lesson. But what he tried to do, he tried to con me
into swapping my horn for his horn.

Now, my horn was a silver-plated with a gold bell -- with a gold plated bell instrument. He had what's called a blue jazz saxophone. It was a -- can't think of the name now -- off brand, and it was painted blue. They called it blue jazz. And he got mad at me because I wouldn't switch, and swap my horn for his horn.
(End of Tape One)

So, I said, well, I don't need a guy like him to be teaching me, you know what I mean, if he was going to try to rob me out of my brand new horn -- and my horn wasn't even paid for -- quite paid for. Do you know what I mean?

So, I went on back and went back to the woodshed, as we called it. Went back to the woodshed and kept on practicing, kept on practicing. So, I got so I could play a few tunes. And the first tune I really learned as 'You can see your momma every night. Can't see your poppa at all (singing).' So, there was a fellow, a drummer named James Morgan -- his nickname was 'Toe' Morgan. 'Toe' Morgan had a job on Christmas Day, 1924. He said, 'Hayes, come on and play this job with us.' I said, 'Toe', I'm not good enough to play with you. He said, 'Man, you can play that one piece and just clap your hands and whatnot.'
And I shall never forget it. I went on that job. I sat up there. I didn't know how to tune my horn. And we

played that piece, and my horn was kind of out of tune but I didn't know how to tune it. And I was clowning and I just, you know, clapped my hands, you know. And I stand up -- you know what I mean -- and pop my fingers. And the people would come by and they'd say, "Oh, your band sounds good," you know what I mean. It was only a piano, drums, and myself.

And I made $5.00. It was a matinee dance in 1924. I shall never forget it as long as I live. And that gave me a little inspiration. And the next job I took, I took a job at a place called Fairman's, which is about six miles outside of town.

And I went to work on this job with a boy named Crump. He was a drummer. And I forget who played the piano, it's been so long ago. And I tried to tune up with the piano and didn't know how to tune up.

To make a long story short, we played that job. And it was on a Saturday night -- I shall never forget it. And back in those days, most every car you rode in was a touring car. So, on my way back home I got in the car -- I was supposed to ride back -- ride back to North Little Rock. And I set up in the car and went to sleep. I had my horn in my lap, and my arm around it. But I had a watch that I had bought. And it was an Elgin watch with a chain on it. And I went to sleep. And when I got home and got out of the car and walked in the house, I realized that someone had stole -- had taken my watch
from me. So, On that job I think I made $5.00 or $6.00, and I lost my watch. My watch at that time cost $30.00. Had a beautiful chain here. Used to wear them across the chest then.

But I kept on practicing and practicing. So, there was a lady named Mrs. Colter. She had a little combo. And I went by to see her about joining her combo. So, Mrs. Colter told me, she says, "Well now, I've got a little job. This job is going to be in about two weeks." She said, "I'm going to give you this music. And if you can play this music, come back. When you come back -- we have rehearsal next week. If you can play this music, I'll give you the job."

And in the meantime she did the same thing to a trumpet player, and told him the same thing. I took that music and I went home, and I practiced that music note to note, note to note. I remember one piece -- one of the piece -- one of the tunes was "Maquita." (Singing) Maquita, Maquita (hum).

Man, I learned how to play that song. I played every song she gave me. It was about seven tunes. And I worked on those tunes, and I worked on them day and night. And that night rehearsal she said, "Come on and tune up." She taught me how to tune my horn. She says, "You are playing a C instrument." I was playing a C melody horn. And it was a C melody -- it was a C instrument.
She says, "Your horn is tuned right with the piano. C instrument." And all I had to do was when she hit A, I hit
my A. And you could tell when I was flat or sharp. I could pull it out or push it in. That's where I learned how to tune up.

And I played --- we had that rehearsal, and I played that music. She said, "Pillars, you've got the job." The other boy came back, and he didn't learn to play his and he didn't get the job. And that gave me a lot of encouragement.

But I would work on it. I would take a piece of music, and I would work on it. I'd just work on it note by note, note by note. Then I got so I could just read it, you know. Then I got to be, as I said, I got to be a sight reader. I got to be an excellent reader, you know what I mean. And I could just read practically anything, you know what I mean. And that's what happened, you know, down through the years.
Was there anybody who helped you with your learning your notes, and learning your rhythms?

Yeah, one boy. There was a boy named -- his name was Wendell Hayman. His father was a doctor. Wendell played the violin -- the violin. I'd go by Wendell's house. And Wendell (unintelligible) and the violin and my C melody saxophone. And Wendell would play. I'd play, and Wendell would say, "No, do it this way. This is the way it is." And Wendell taught me -- he really gave me my fundamentals, because he was a very fine musician. And then I had a chance to join with Wendell -- he recommended me joining the Royal City

Orchestra. Royal The Roll City Orchestra was a band that had been formed by a guy named Sterling Todd, who was a great piano player. And Sterling Todd had left Arkansas and gone to Chicago, you know what I mean, to further his professional, you know what I mean, career.

And so, we would have rehearsals. And I'd sit right next to Wendell, and as Wendell would play -- we would practice -- I'd go right over to his practically at (unintelligible) house practically every day. I'd practice with Wendell. And I got to be a good reader, see.
And this particular band, the Roll City Ban Royal d, we would play dates in Hot Springs and different cities, you know, around in a 50, 60 miles radius, 75 miles radius of Little Rock.
Was this before or after the lady helped you to join her organization?
This was after. This was after. This was after, see. This was more -- a more progressive, professional group than this lady had, see.
I see.
This lady, she was a nice musician, see, but she didn't get too many jobs, you know.
Uh-huh.
But if she could get a job, you know what I mean, she would let you know maybe two, three weeks in

advance, and she'd let you rehearse and prepare for it, see. But then I got so I could read with this group. And we would go to Hot Springs, Arkansas. And this I want to will tell you, because they didn't have nightclubs back in that day. And here's what they would do.

In the wintertime rich people would come to Hot Springs. I can remember Babe Ruth would come down to Hot Springs in the wintertime. And the millionaires would come down. And what they would do, we would play a dance at the Pythiqn Bath House, and all of these whites would come over to the Pythiqn Bath House. And the promoter (unintelligible) would feature cake walking, a dancers' forum dance (unintelligible). And there were various couples, you know what I mean, they would do cake walk dancing, Professor. And here's how they would do.

There was a tune written like this (sings). And the cake walk they would -- you would walk fast like that. They would bend down and you bow, and they had the long dresses, you know, and they had the big hats, you know. And the woman moment would grab the her partner's arms, you know. And they would skip through, you know. And that was the cake walk.

All those people would pay a lot of money, you know what I mean. The promoter would promote that, see. And about -- during the season about twice a month, And we would go over there and play those dances . So, they'd have a cake walking contest, see, and they would have maybe about five or

six couples. And they would, you know, have them to pick out the winner. Put your hand over one couple, and the loudest applause -- you know what I mean -- they would give them a prize, see. And that was the popular mode of entertainment for those people back in the 20's. That was late -- that was late -- that was early -- that was late '24 and early '25.

And this same -- a buddy of mine, the fellow who got me that first job I told you about, "Toe" Morgan. His name was James "Toe" Morgan. He had a job in Jackson, Tennessee, and asked me did I want to go over to Jackson, Tennessee, and join the Johnnie Brown's orchestra. Johnnie Brown and his Playtone Orchestra.

This was a time when I told you that I left home. And my mother told me she was going to let me leave home. And that all she would ask of me was to be a good boy, and use common sense, and think of your mother while you're away. And this I did. And I joined Johnnie Brown's Playtone Orchestra. I arrived there on a Sunday, and we left Monday morning for Mississippi..
Where was this again?
Jackson, Tennessee. Jackson, Tennessee.

We left the Monday morning for Mississippi, on the Illinois Central. Oxford, Mississippi was where the University of Mississippi is located. This was my first town -- my first time playing in the state of Mississippi.

I can remember it was around 100 miles from Jackson because the fare back in those days was $3.00 a hundred. Our fare was $3.00 apiece. We arrived in Oxford, Mississippi. It was a quaint, old Southern city. No sidewalks. Dusty streets. They had a walkway from the station. They had a big frame walkway from the station, because there was a great big ravine or a gully in front of the station. They had a great big walkway from the station uptown about-- I guess about a block and a half. And this was a big frame walkway -- you had bannisters -- you know, you could walk up to town, see.

I remember, after we got in town. And we had a regular place. Johnnie Brown had been playing through that territory for years. We had a regular place where we would room. And I got up, and I walked around in town, looked the city over. It was just about one or two blocks. And it was no sidewalks at that time. Dusty streets. That was the summer of 1925.

We played Oxford, Mississippi. We left there and went to Water Valley -- I think it was Water Valley, and several other cities. We headed on down to Granada, Mississippi, into the delta which was Greenwood. And the delta was the most lucrative part of Mississippi so far as bands were concerned. It seemed like the people in the delta had just a little bit more money to spend than the people elsewhere. And the delta started at Greenwood, and you went through (unintelli-
on down through Indianola, down into Greenville on the Mississippi. Then you had Yazoo City. And you had other towns in Mississippi.

And so, we played those cities. We would go out and stay out maybe a week, a week and a half, then come back to Jackson. Then we'd spend a couple, two or three days. Then we would go down to Corinth, Mississippi, which was on the M&O. That was a different route, see. And going into Tupelo, Mississippi; Okolona, Mississippi; into towns like West Point, Mississippi. And, of course, Starkville, Mississippi, and Aberdeen. And then we'd come back to Tupelo, and we'd go back over west to New Albany, Mississippi.

And so, I used to keep a diary of all these cities that we played, see. And I can remember in Corinth -- we played in Corinth, and that was where the Battle of Shiloh was fought on the Tennessee River. And I made a special trip out there to see where General Johnson was shot, and the tree where he died when they laid him up against a tree where he died. And that to me, that was American history, you know, that I wanted to see with my own eyes.

And I played with Johnn Brown almost all of that summer, until the latter part of August. I was offered a job by a gentleman named Gordon C. Harrison, who was a great pianist, and he lived in Texacana, Texas. They were opening a new hotel in Texacana called the Grimm Hotel, and this hotel

was built right on the state line. It was a brand new, beautiful hotel. And Gordon C. Harrison had heard about me, and they sent me a ticket. And I left Johnnie Brown's band, and I went to Texicana. I called my mother and them up and told them I'd be through Little Rock that evening, and they came over to the railroad station to say hi to me. And the train must have spent about 15 minutes there, and I passed through Little Rock going to Texicana.

I arrived in Texicana and I joined this band. This was my first exposure to playing in a big, fine hotel where we had to play lunch -- luncheon music every day at noon, and dinner music every evening from 6:00 to 8:30.
Excuse me. You mentioned that this man had heard about you.

Yeah, he had heard about me, yes. He had heard about me through musicians who had played with the Royal City Band. You see, those communities are small communities, you know, see. Little Rock was only 140 miles -- less than 140 miles from Texicana. And he had organized this band with some musicians from Little Rock, and they knew me, see. And they recommended me to him, and he sent me a wire and he offered me a nice salary. I think the salary was $35.00 a week.
Had you developed into a soloist at this point?
Oh, yes. I was -- man, I was playing--
I had changed from a C melody to an alto saxophone then.
So, he'd heard about you and this (inaudible).

See, and he heard about me. See, what -- you see, the advantage I had in playing a C melody, I knew all the keys that a piano would play in. Then when I bought the alto saxophone, that gave me an advantage of playing in the sharps -- more sharps, see. And then in later years when I started playing the tenor saxophone, that gave me the advantage of playing in the flat keys, which I was used to when I was playing the C instrument, see.

And so, when pieces would come out in D flat -- when D flat -- when "Stardust" first came out, "Stardust was one of the first tunes to come out in D flat. Well, to me, that was just like throwing the rabbit in the brain patch (unintelligible). I could play in D flat. Most tenor saxophone players couldn't play in D flat because it was a new key to them.
Uh-huh.
But I could play in practically all of the keys, because I had played three different instruments which familiarized me with these various keys.
Right.
Okay. I joined the Gordon C. Harrison Band. We had two saxophones. The first saxophonist's name was Alvin Fat Walls. Alvin Fat Walls was a virtuoso on the
saxophone. He was a virtuoso. He just died recently a few years ago in Detroit.

Alvin Fat Walls was a soloist. I played the second part -- you know what I mean -- or the third part, see. And I had a good ear, and tunes that they didn't have the second part to, I could fake the harmony and just play right on with it, see.

And this is where I first learned of the dignity of the bandstand, and how it should be conducted when you're playing dinner music and when you're playing for luncheons and things -- you know what I mean. You're supposed to be well-dressed, and well-mannered, and you play beautiful music, and you play soft music. And on the bandstand we weren't allowed to talk, because we were in a dining room, see. And the main purpose for us was to be incidental. Play pretty music and play soft, so the public -- the patrons rather could sit and converse and enjoy their food, and enjoy the music -- you know what I mean -- musical background.

And this is where I really received most of my education in the mannerism of dinner music and things like that, see. And it really stuck with me the rest of my life. And Alvin Fat Walls could play beautiful solos. He'd play all the classics. And he played them beautifully. And the public was just crazy about him.
Only day Alvin Fat Walls had to go home because his

mother was ill or something. And so, I had to play the first saxophone. I did well. One piece I played -- I tried to play it like Alvin. And it had a high note. I tried to hit the high note, and the high note didn't come out. And it come out a little squeak.

After we got through playing, the band leader called me over. He said, "Hayes, let me tell you something." He says, "If you're going to be a professional musician, you never attempt to hit a note unless you know that you can make that note." He says, "Because if you attempt to hit a note and you don't make that note, you sound like an amateur. You're not a professional." This I never forgot. This I never forgot down through the years.

And I'm just indebted to Mr. Harrison for the patience -- you know what I mean -- and the little small things that he taught me -- or rather he taught us. He was a graduate from the American Conservatory of Music in Chicago.
I stayed with him until the job ran out.
What year was this.
That was in 19 -- that was part of 1925 too.
Was this man white?
Huh?
Was this man white?
He was colored.
And he was a graduate of American at that time?
He was a graduate of American Conservatory of Music.
That was quite a milestone for a black man at that time.

Oh, yes, sir. And in that city he knew all of the millionaires, all of the big oil people. They were all crazy about Gordon C. Harrison. And Gordon C. Harrison, what he would do, between numbers he would play the classics. He played the beautiful classics. Then he would play -- tape it off with Victor Herbert -- you know what I mean -- his songs. Like "Kiss Me Again" and those type of songs, you know what I mean. And he played so beautifully. And the people would just sit at the table and just "Oh" -- you know what I mean -- at this artist.

Well, this was the man that really broke me in, and that taught me the mannerisms -- you know what I mean -- of -- or the dynamics of music, and how you should tone your music down -- you know what I mean. In other words, you play according to the occasions. And I never forgot it.

That job gave out, and Gordon Harrison -- we brought the band back to Little Rock, and we worked in and out and around Little Rock for a while. And then Gordon decided, well, he's going back home. So, he -- the band bursted up. But that

saxophone player was Alvin Pat Walls.
He later went to Texas and had a band of his own.
And then he finally left Texas. He went to Detroit, and he
played with some of the fine bands around Detroit. Fletcher
Henderson offered him a job many years ago and -- because he
was supposed to have been the only man that sat in Fletcher
Henderson's band and played every note by sight. Because back
in those days Fletcher Henderson was playing a lot of hard
music, and in a lot of hard keys back in those days.

I'll tell you a story about Fletcher Henderson that
happened in 1920 -- early -- in '27, the summer of '27 -- a
little bit later on, you see. Gordon C. Harrison came on --
he left Little Rock and went on back to Texicana, and a year or
two later he went to California. And he worked at a burlesque
theater out there until he died. I forget what year he died,
but he died, oh, about 30 some years ago he died out there.

I left Little Rock and went back to Johnn Brown,
and played with Johnn Brown through '25, through '26 into
'27, and left him in '27 and went back to Little Rock. And
while playing with Johnn Brown, I found Johnn Brown to be
a great clarinetist. In his home he had pasted his instructor
all over his walsl -- around the walls, see. And he would
practice -- he would just walk around the wall and just play
this different -- you know, different lessons that he had
played, you know, years ago. And he'd warm up -- that's the way
he would warm up every day, see. A great artist.

This man was a great clarinetist, and a fine gentleman. He helped me along. He was of a high caliber man. And back in those days, Sam, the entertainment for people in Mississippi and Arkansas -- the only entertainment they had was through shows like the Rabbit Foot Minstrel, and shows like the Silas Green Minstrel.

Now, these shows would play these various cities every year. Both shows would play. Like one would come in, maybe play the early part of the year. One would come in and play -- and usually -- sometimes they would play a little bit after the crops had -- you know what I mean -- come through and the people would have a little money, see.
And there was one show that had a little young saxophonist and clarinetist named Lewis Joy. I guess you've heard of Lewis Joy. Louis Jordan.
Sure.

Well, Lewis Jordan and I were around about the same age. Louis Jordan -- I first saw Louis Jordan, he was playing with the Rabbit Foot Minstrel. He was one of the greatest -- he was one of the most exciting musicians I had ever heard at that time. He played the clarinet and the soprano saxophone. Well, the soprano saxophone was rather a new instrument, you know, back in that time. And Louis Jordan could play both instruments, the clarinet and the soprano saxo-

phone. I mean when he would take that saxophone and put it up in the air, the people would just scream. The people just went crazy. He was an artist. He always has been an artist. He was born in Brinkley, Arkansas.
And that was my first time meeting Louis Lewis Jordan.

And with the Silas Green Minstrel I met a very fine clarinetist, one of the great clarinetists of the race at that time. His name was Bob Young. Bob Young was from Bolivar, Tennessee. That's a little town a few miles below Jackson, Tennessee, between Jackson and Holly Spring, Mississippi, but still in Tennessee.

This man played all of the clarinet concertos and whatnot. And he played them out of this world. I had never heard such music played by individuals in all my life at that time. It was a great experience traveling around with Johnnie Y Brown and his Playtone Orchestra.
(End of Tape Two)

We used to take trips up into northern Alabama. We played towns like Sheffield, Alabama; Tuscumbia, Alabama; Florence, Alabama; Decatur, Alabama; Athens, Alabama; Huntsville, Alabama. That was northern Alabama.

One tune in particular -- one town in particular we played in was Florence, Alabama. Florence was across the Tennessee River from Sheffield, Alabama. and in Florence there was a pool hall where we used to go and hang out and play pool
in the afternoons. And there was a house next door to the pool hall. And this house was where W. C. Handy was born. Florence, Alabama.
And I would walk out and look at the house, you know. And I just said, 'Well, at least I saw the house where he was born in Florence, Alabama.'

We ventured out one year through northern Alabama, up to Chattanooga, Tennessee, and we got stranded in Chattanooga, Tennessee. We were stopping at a hotel called the Dent Hotel. And this is one of the reasons why I love people today, because people have been good to me all my life. When I say me, I mean good to us musicians all of our lives.

We stayed in that hotel. We didn't have money to pay for food -- to pay for food. And Mr. Dent, everytime that dinnertime come, he'd say, 'Come on, boys, and sit at the table. Come on out here and eat.' And he would feed us. And I can remember how we got out of that town. We had two saxophones in the band then. We had a boy named Philander Tiller from Little Rock who I had recommended to join the band. Fernando Tiller had been going to Howard University, and this particular year he had laid out of school.

So, in order to get out of town, Johnny Brown booked our band back to Sheffield, Alabama. And the only way he could do it was to take Phil Tiller's saxophone and ask him would it be all right for us to pawn his horn -- pawn Tiller's horn, and

let Tiller stay there.
And we would go to Sheffield, Alabama where Johnnie Brown had friends, and we had booked ourselves in there for several dances in and around Sheffield. And we pawned the horn for enough money to pay our train fare from there to Sheffield.
As luck would have it,
(Unintelligible) we played a big dance there. We had a big crowd. And Johnnie Brown was able to borrow money from one of the big business people there. He wired the money to Phil Tiller, paid up our bill there, and sent Phil Tiller a ticket to come and join us. And these were the things you had to do back in those days, you know what I mean, when things got rough on you.
Things were really rough back in those days. You didn't make much money, but we all loved each other and we stuck together.
In 1927 I left Johnnie Brown. I went back home. While being back home I started to work with a band named Brady Bryant and his Merrymakers. In that band we had Mr. Brady Bryant -- he played the drums -- and a fellow named George Lot played trumpet. Another fellow named Carl Charleson played trumpet. I played the alto saxophone. And by that time Louis Jordan had left the show, and he was back in Little Rock. So, Louis Jordan and I had a chance to play together in this band.

There was a white promoter in Mississippi who thought enough of the band to buy two Chevrolet touring cars and turn them over to us for transportation. Now, he booked us all through Mississippi. And we played dances all through Mississippi. I mean we played Cleveland, Mississippi; Belzoni; many towns.

And in the meantime, we look in the newspaper, Chicago Defender, and we read where Fletcher Henderson was finishing his engagement at the Congress Hotel. And he was going to play a one night stand at the Chicago Armory that summer -- I can't think of the date, but it was during the same week that Dempsey fought Tunney -- that was before you was born, Doc.
Right. Do you remember the year?
Uh-huh.

So, we had terminated our working agreement with this white fellow in Greenwood, Mississippi, and we had a manager -- his name was Sweet Davis. Sweet Davis was a big gambler, and he always had a pocketful of money. And he drove a great, big seven-passenger Studebaker touring car.
So, Sweet Davis said, 'You little so-and-sos, you're

all talking about you want to go to Chicago, you want to do this. I'll tell you what you do." He says, "If you give me $10.00 apiece, I'll drive you to Chicago and I'll bring you back." He wanted to go to Chicago himself, see.
Right.

So, we said, "Okay, okay." So, we had a few jobs to play. We played the jobs and gave him the money. So, we hopped in the car. We got our bags to gether, and we hit it out for Chicago. We got in Missouri -- I forget the little town. It was only just above the Arkansas line. And we -- the driving rod broke -- the Studebaker. So, we had to wait all night and the next day -- we had to wait a day and a half to get the part. We had it put in. So, we headed out for Chicago.

And we got to Chicago. And the Chicago Defender, they gave us free tickets to go to that affair. And Doc, I was the happiest person in the world, because I had all my life -- see, Fletcher Henderson's band was the hottest band out at that time, see. His band had been hot from the early 20's on up when he made "Sugarfoot Stomp." That was when Louis Armstrong was playing with him, and he made that famous recording -- Fletcher Henderson -- the "Sugarfoot Stomp." That was the piece that introduced him to America, "Sugarfoot Stomp."
Okay. Fletcher Henderson. We all went down to the Chicago Armory. I can name every member of that band right now.

His reed section was Buster Bailey on alto sax and clarinet. He had Jerome Pascual playing alto sax and clarinet. Coleman Hawkins played the tenor saxophone. Trumpet -- he had Russell Smith playing first trumpet. Joe Smith was playing second trumpet, and a fellow named Tommy Ladnier playing third trumpet and he was the get off man.
What was his last name?

Tommy Ladnier. He was a hot trumpet player out of New York at that time. On trombone he had a fellow named Moten. I just can't think of Moten's first name, but Moten played a beautiful trombone. In later years Moten made the original "One O'Clock Jump" with Count Basie. And he played the original -- the first solo played on "One O'Clock Jump" Moten played that with the Count Basie Band.
This is no relation to Bennie Moten?

No. No relation at all. And Jimmy Harrison Hash, trombone. Jimmy Hash was from Louisville, Kentucky. Great trombonist. He died young. On drums he had a fellow named Kaiser. Kaiser was the one that introduced the hand cymbal. Just played drums and used to have a hand cymbal, and you could play them with sticks. You know, he introduced that effect, the hand cymbal effect.
(June Cole - ed.)
That was the -- the bass player -- I can't remember his name. But the rest of those fellows -- and I met them all, and I talked with them, and I got to be a great friend of
Buster BAiley and a great friend of Coleman Hawkins before he died.

But that trip, that was a great trip. And I shall never forget it because that was the week that Tunney beat Dempsey in Chicago. Chicago was Chicago then. That was when South Parkway was South Parkway, a beautiful street. And as you got along where the parks were, they had the tennis courts all the way up to 60 -- to 60th Street, I think it was. That was 1927.

We get back home. Come October of 1927 -- I think it was the 4th of October -- that was when I joined the great Alphonso Trent's band. This band was one of the greatest black bands, I think, ever assembled. This band had gone to Texas about two years before that time, had gotten a job working at the Adolphus Hotel, which was owned at that time by the Anheiser Busch people. They went in waited there for a two weeks engagement, and stayed there 14 months. And they broadcasted from station WFAA, one of the first times a black group ever broadcasted that long -- you know, from a fine hotel.

They played everything you could think of: dinner music; they played hot music; they played -- they had a glee club in the band. This was the band that Jimmy ie Lunceford heard in Memphis, Tennessee in October of 1927 that inspired him. This is the band that he mentioned to a French magazine writer that he got his inspiration from the Alphonso Trent's band.

I joined that band, and I found out that all of our arrangements were head arrangements. They would take a tune and start rehearsing it, and everybody'd put their idea in it and sometimes they would be a week rehearsing one tune. But they rehearsed every day. And each day somebody would come up with different ideas. With different ideas.

And in the brass section they had a trio singing, and in the reed section we had a trio singing. Then we all sang together as a choral group. We had novelties. We could clown. We did everything. We would play a dance -- back in those days you'd play a dance, and the people just wouldn't dance. They just stand around the band watch the band. And practically every man in the band was a great artist. I'll call off some of the names of this great band.
I understand that you and your brother were the mainstays of that -- the reed section of Alphonso Trent's Treble's band.
Well --
Along with --
Jeeter.
-- Jeeter.

Along with Jeeter. Yeah, see. Well, I'll tell you what happened. See, we had a boy -- a saxophone player named Lee Hillard. He was from Seguin, Texas. He died I guess about 10 years ago, I hear. He was a great alto

saxophonist, and he also played trumpet. Lee Hillard and James Jeter, and myself were the reed section back in those days. And my brother joined the band in the 30's. This was in '27. My brother joined the band -- my brother joined the band in -- oh, let's see, 1930 -- he joined the band in '32, I think it was. '31 or '32.
I see.

I think it was '32. He joined the band in '32, Oklahoma City. Yeah. We had a boy named Edwin Swayzee; Swayzee was from Little Rock. He played trumpet. Beautiful trumpet. Swayzee left Trent's band and he joined Cab Calloway's band, and he played with Cab Calloway's band until he died. He died young. He died young. He died in the early -- he died in the 30's.

And we had a boy named Chester Clark who played a beautiful trumpet, beautiful tone. Everybody had big tones in this band. They could play waltzes. They could play that pretty music, and could play hot music too. Also had a boy in the band named Herbert "Peanuts" Holland. Peanuts played with Trent's band. He was what you call a hot jazz trumpet player. He could play high. He could -- he played -- he was exciting to hear. He left Trent's band and he joined -- I'll recall his name in a minute.
Anyway Peanuts Holland -- I was in Stockholm, Sweden -- that's where he'd lived for years -- and I was there in '71.
I looked him up but I couldn't find him. But I hear that he's back there and he's been sick. I hear that he's back there and he's been sick. Oh, he played with Charlie Barnett's orchestra.
Peanut played with Charlie Barnett's orchestra until the band disbanded. I think he played with that band about eight years.

Leo "Snub" Mosley. A trombonist. He was through here about a month and a half ago. "Snub" Mosley played trombone and the slide saxophone. He is the only living person in the world today who plays a slide saxophone.
Can you describe that instrument?

Yes, sir. It's got a round bell like this. And this -- the bell's big here, and it comes up small like here, see. And it's got holes in it, see. It's got holes in it. And there's a slide that goes up, see. And it's got a crook in it, see. And they blows it and it sounds like a soprano saxophone, see. But you get your tone from sliding it up and down. And this horn must have come out, oh, back in the 20's and it never was popular, see. And I think Snub bought the last one that the factory had made before the factory went out of business.
And he was here. He's got a lot of nerve. He's an extrovert, this guy. He'll take his horn out and play it anywhere, see. And my brother and I -- when I see him, he was just

passing through, going back to New York. He had been to Little Rock to see his father. And he stopped. He was sitting at the airport and we saw him. He pulled his saxophone out and played a little tune for us, you know. And people started gathering around. Then he gave us pictures where he had played tunes for the Queen of England this past summer during the Centennial -- you know what I mean. I think she had visited up in Harlem. I think it was at Aaron Burr's home or someone's home up in Holland there.

And the Queen had it roped off. And Snub Mosley played this solo to her, and she shook his hand, see. He gave me a picture. I should have brought that picture along with me. I would like for you to have seen it, see.
Does he still play that slide saxophone?

Oh, yeah. Yeah. He still plays it, yeah. That's one of his features, yeah. And he has a combo. He plays in all the smart clubs and things in, I believe, New York, New Jersey, around. He's well known in musical circles. Snub Mosley.

Of course, James Jeeter was -- James Jeeter, my partner, was the first alto player. He never did play any hot saxophone, but he played first saxophone. Lee Hilliard -- I mentioned him -- Lee Hilliard. There was A. G. Godley who played the drums. A. G. Godley wrote a book on drums. He
never was able to get it published. But this man was every bit an artist.

Now, he played music until he just got -- he couldn't make the money that he wanted to make. He joined the Merchant Marines -- you know what I mean. And he traveled in the ships and whatnot, and he retired out in Seattle. And he died about three and a half years ago. But he was a very fine drummer. He knew all the fundamentals of timpani and all like that. He was a great drummer. He was a great friend of the great black drummer in New York, what's his name? Cozy --
Cozy Cole?

Cozy Cole. They were just like that. They both were technicians. The same type technician. They were great friends. We had a banjo player named Eugene Crooke in Trent's band. Eugene Crooke was a great banjo player. And he was a tall fellow, thick sideburns. And he and Leo loved each other but they never could get along. They was fighting each other like cats and dogs. They would argue all the time, see, in the band, see. They never fought each other but they just -- they never could get along. But if one was in trouble, one would go down there -- they would, you know -- they would give their heart, you know --
Right.
-- for each other. Yes, uh-huh. There was a bass horn player named Ben Sparks. Ben Sparks was a

great -- he was an old, ex-show circusman, a great bass horn player. He died in Indianapolis, oh, back in the early 30's. Sy Oliver joined our band in 1930. Alphonso Trent let him front the band, because he was writing for the band. He had been writing for Zach White, who he started out with in Cincinnati. Well, you've heard of Zach White, haven't you?
Sure.

Zach White's band in Cincinnati. And he had met the great arranger from McKinney's Cotton Pickers, John Nesbitt. John Nesbitt was the man -- John Nesbitt and Don Redman were the two arrangers that set the style and pace for swing music back in the 20's, late 20's. They did more than any other persons to style the swing music back in that day. More about him a bit later on.
We had another bass player that joined us named Epicurean. Epicurean was -- he played bass horn like you play a trumpet. Genius.
Epicurean?
Epicurean. That's the name that they gave him because he could eat. That's the name he -- he assumed this name. I don't know any other name.
I was wondering if there was some significance to it.
He assumed that name because he could eat more than anybody -- anybody else ever hear of. That's
the kind of guy he was.
Uh-huh.
Epicurean. He died, oh, I guess about 20- some 27 years ago up in Jefferson City, the state of Missouri. Now, the prize of our band was Stuff Smith. You ever hear of him?
Sure.
Fiddle player.
Violinist, uh-huh.

Stuff Smith. He was born in Portsmouth, Ohio. Stuff and I -- he joined Trent's Treb's band in Lexington, Kentucky in 1927, the fall of 1927. Stuff Smith joined our band then. And after he played, you know, on the bandstand with us, Alphonso Trent Treb took Stuff and put him out front, and then direct the band and played the fiddle. And he was a genius. A great musician, a great ear. And, oh, man, he was just tops.

And Stuff and myself, we -- at times we used to room together, you know. And we would get our -- he would get his fiddle out and I'd get my horn out, and we -- all we thought of was, you know, playing music. We just played practically all day. We just played all day, you know. And we enjoyed it, see. Great guy.
There was another guy named Irving Ervin Randolph from St. Louis. Irving Ervin Randolph -- I don't know where he was born, but we met him here in St. Louis. He joined our band back in '28.
Beautiful trumpet player. Cab Calloway took him too. Now, I don't know where he is now, see. I'm just giving you a taste of the caliber of musicians that we had at that time.

In later years when the band started kind of disintegrating a little bit, we picked up a guy named Gus Wilson. Gus Wilson was the brother of Teddy Wilson. Gus Wilson was a genius. But it seems as though in the family his father had always thrown up Teddy to Gus -- "Why don't you be like Teddy?" And this --
Was Gus a pianist too?

No, Gus was a trombone player. He could play piano. Trombone player. And he was an kind-of arranger. And he was a modern arranger back in those days. He could write like mad. But he was the type of guy if you said, "Gus, that was a beautiful (unintelligible) solo," he'd get up and walk off the bandstand because he'd think you was trying to jive him, you know, kid him. And he had that little mental problem, see. And he left his mother -- his father had died, and his mother lived up in Des Moines, Iowa, I think. And he left and went up there, and shortly after that he died.

Well, I have nothing but pleasant memories being around him because he knew music, and he was a genius. But there was just something about him that he just -- he just couldn't make it. He just couldn't make it. It was a tragic thing about his life.
Well, that was Alphonso Trent's band. Let's see, do I have anything -- I think I covered the highlights of, you know, most of the guys in the band.
Uh-huh.

We -- in Trent's band -- we left Little Rock and went our way north, seeking our -- you know, seeking our fortune. You know what I mean? We played Memphis, Tennessee. That's how we (unintelligible) Jimmy Lunceford. We went on and played on around through Jackson, Tennessee; on through Nashville; on up into Louisville, Kentucky.
There was a guy I knew of in Kentucky named Hurley. He was a red cap for Union Station, but he was a band promoter. He promoted all of the bands there at that time. His name was Hurley.
What year was this?

That was 1927. That was '27. And we settled in Louisville with this band. And the guys had their wives -- you know what I mean -- whatnot -- those who were married. So, we set out to look for some, you know, jobs and work.

So, there was a guy -- there was a fellow in town, a musician in town who at one time had been real popular, you know, around town. His name was Lockwood Lewis. Lockwood Lewis. This was a very beautiful man. This was a beautiful
person. Lockwood Lewis helped us get a job in a roadhouse up on the Ohio River. I think that's the Ohio River there in Louisville.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
