It's up on the Ohio River, this roadhouse. And we took this job and back in those days, you know, that was during the days of Prohibition -- people'd come out and they would eat and, of course, whether they were serving liquor, I don't know, but they -- they were drinking at the tables, you know what I mean, you see? And the job paid us $25.00 a week. And that little job kept us together when we got in Louisville for a few weeks.

So we decided to book some dates in Lexington, Kentucky. And this we did. We booked our band in Lexington, Kentucky, and we played a big dance there and the band was such a big riot, you know, so we booked another date there, I think, about 10 days later. Well the owners of the Roseland Ballroom had heard about us and they came out and heard the band. They heard the band and they offered us a job. Working at this ballroom in Lexington. And this must've been latter part of November, I guess, in November.

So we were happy to get this job, it was a lifesaver. We took this job, and we worked every night except Sundays. So, the Sundays gave us a chance to book the band over in Cincinnati, on a Sunday night dance. And would give us a chance to play at the Crystal Ballroom there, or else play at the Sterling Hotel. And so the band started going up there, playing every Sunday night, and man the band -- the

band was a riot in Cincinnati. Well Cincinnati turned out to be the hub city for bands. You know, all bands would come into Cincinatti, you know. Come from the East, they come from the West, from the South or Southeast or Southwest, you know? And you always you -- had bands coming in. And there were bands like Speed Steve Webb, -- Speed Webb's band. He had a band from Indiana, that's where I first met Teddy Wilson.

And Roy Eldridge, they were kids, youngsters then, see? And Roy Eldridge had a brother who played alto sax. They all played with Speed Webb's band. And there was a local band there named West Halvey. Wes Halvey had a trombone player named Vic Dickenson Dixon, Vic Dickerson is a -- one of your top jazz trombone players, today. I hear that he's out in Denver and some rich jazz enthusiast had him be move out there and he just takes care of him, you know what I mean?

Vic just, you know, plays for this guy, and he plays, you know what I mean, a few jazz clubs around -- around Denver. This is what I heard a year or two ago, and -- I don't know where Vic is now, he may be there and he may not be.

But, there was another band, a beautiful band, now. Alex Jackson. Alex Jackson was from originally from Dallas, Texas. He was a school teacher and he had a band out there, they played at a lot of the white clubs in Cincinnati, and all of them were clean-cut fellas, you know what I mean. But

then they decided to - Alex Jackson decided to go back to Dallas and teach school and the band just gradually -- just melted away, you see? But, many bands would come into Cincinnati and they would lay-over there, you know what I mean? And they would loaf there and then they would -- somewhat -- they would break-up there, a lot of times bands would -- a lot of bands were formed there, see. But that's the story of Cincinnati, Ohio.

This Lockwood fella, Lockwood Lewis, there was a lady in Louisville, named Miss Bessie Allen. And she was a self-styled social worker, back in those days they didn't have social workers, you know, per se, you know. But she was a lady that was always trying to do something, for you know, the youth and the community. And she went to Lockwood Lewis and asked him would he teach the kids if she formed a children's band? And this he did.

And he and this lady worked diligently and formed this children's band years ago there in Louisville, Kentucky. And the end result was that quite a few musicians came out that band and they went on and furthered their profession in music. That's why I mentioned the fact that this Lockwood Lewis was a very beautiful person, see? I think when he died, he was driving a cab, you know, man, for the City Cab Company, there when he died.
Out of Louisville came such saxophone players like
Bob Carroll, do you know of him, Bob Carroll? No.
Bob Carroll played tenor with Don Redman, when Don Redman had his great band.
Uh-huh.

And Jonah Jones George Owens, and another fella that -- that played -- that played in and around there, Dick Wells. Trombone player, you may know of him? And you may not. Dick Wells. There was another band out of Springfield, Ohio, that used to play through Cincinnati, into Louisville, and this band was Cecil Scott. Had a brother named Lloyd Scott. Cecil Scott was a baritone saxophone player, he was a terrific musician. They Tell me he jumped out of a window or something in New York and he broke one of his legs and I think the leg had to be amputated and in later years he died. I think his brother -- his brother Lloyd Scott, they're all dead now. But back in the '20's, they were well known through that part of the country.

I mentioned Speed Webb, you know, and -- the -- Teddy Wilson and those guys, worked in the band. You know, back in 1927, we would go and play dances in Indianapolis, Indiana. And there was a little nightclub there, where they would, you know, hired bands and I should never forget when I first met Claude Hopkins, you know Claude Hopkins, don't you? The band leader? Claude Hopkins?
: Where was he from?

He was from Washington, D. C. Claude Hopkins. Claud Hopkins, had a big band, he'd broadcast on the networks back in -- oh, back in the '30's. In the '30's, Orlando Robeson was a great singer with him. And made the "Trees" popular he used to sing that over and over -- and that used to come three or four afternoons a week out of New York. Anyway I met Claude Hopkins when he called himself the Six Gingersnaps, I thought perhaps you might've known them. That was back in 1927.

There was a Walker Theater there, which shows like Blanche Calloway, the sister of Cab Calloway, used to bring in shows there at the Walker Theater, that was -- that was dance teams, the dance team of Rector and Cooper, one of the greatest dance teams back in that era. And comedians like Roscoe Conklin Simmons, who was the son of the late Roscoe -- you remember, Roscoe Simmons the great orator? You've heard of him, haven't you?
: Yeah, sure.
Yeah, well it was his son.
: Uh-huh.
I thought I'd mention that, you know? Getting back to St. Louis, Missouri, St. Louis has had quite a history, you know --
: Let me ask you a question before you
Yes?
During this time you were in the Cincinnati-Louisville Area, you were with the --
Alphonso Trent band.
Okay. And when you left there did you come back to St. Louis?

When we left -- here's the way it happened. We closed the Roseland Ballroom, the Spring of 1928. We left there and went to Cincinnati, and we played at the Greystone Ballroom, weekends, like Wednesday, Friday and Saturday, -- Wednesday, Saturday and Sunday, for about -- a month and a half. Then we opened up at the Arcadia Ballroom in Buffalo, New York. And we stayed in Buffalo, New York with Alphonso Trent's band -- we stayed in Buffalo, New York about -- about a month and a half. We stayed there until the Spring.

In Spring of the year, Fate Marable, a bandleader, in St. Louis, wrote us and asked us would we like to come to St. Louis to play on the boat, for the Stee[k]fuss Steamboat Line. And we said yes. And we came back to St. Louis, and went to work on the steamer, St. Paul. And we stayed here that whole summer.
Uh-huh.
That was the Summer of '28. And,

Swazey still worked with us - this fella Swayzee, I told you who left and went with -- with Cab Calloway. We finished the season, we took the boat to Davenport, Iowa, for drydock, then the band had a little recess -- for vacation, and a group of us went to Chicago, that's where I had a chance to first hear Earl Hines at the Apex Club, playing piano with Jimmy Noone. Earl Hines had just made those records with Jimmy Noone, and his name had just popped up in 1928.
Uh-huh.

His records were hot then. And, I ran into Louis Armstrong, who was playing trumpet at the Savoy Ballroom in the Carroll Dickerson's band. Carroll Dickerson was a fiddle player. And Louis Armstrong was playing in the band with Carroll Dickerson.
Was this still in 1928?
That's still 1928.
Uh-huh.

And there was a band here named Floyd Campbell, that used to -- he and a promoter used to bring Louis Armstrong down here on Sunday, evenings Sunday -- Sunday afternoons to play at the Paradise Ballroom, with -- with Floyd Campbell's band. And they would pay him, I think, $100.00 to come down and play those three hours, you know. And go back to Chicago, see. In the meantime, Floyd Campbell had a piano player, that who had formerly played with me, with us
in Jackson, Tennessee, named Gus Perryman. And Gus Perryman was crazy about the Scott Joplin tunes back in that era and he played those tunes even way back then. Gus Pearman did.

And, the Fall of 1928, I'm just trying to think, where did we go then? I think the band went -- yes, after we finished on the boat there in 1928, had a little vacation in Chicago, that's where I told you I met Dr. Charles L. Cook and his band, at the White City? White City Park, at 63rd and South Park? He had a band of great musicians, he was well thought of at that time.

And we left Chicago and came on back through St. Louis and we went on back through ARkansas into Texas and we played -- we played one-nighters, we spent like a couple of weeks in Dallas, played like maybe a couple of dances, kind of like old homecoming week, see? Because the band, you know, had originally started down there. Everybody would go out and see their old friends, this was my first trip with the band that far in Texas.

There's a little dancehall I call the Humming Bird, we played the Humming Bird and we'd just pack them in. And, of course, those are pretty fat days for us. We were making on the average of $40.00, $45.00, sometimes $50.00 a night. When we played, see. On the average sometimes two -- twice a week, sometimes three times a week. And we had a booking agent named Goldberg down there that booked us at A&M University,

down at Bryant, Texas. We played the proms for them, we played at -- at University of Texas at -- University of Texas at Austin, Texas. We opened in Texas -- we opened the new Athletic Building there, I think it was a big gym house there, the first time they ever had an affair in there, our band played for it. That's been years ago. It was a brand new building then, I remember.

We played Orange, Texas, at the countryclub there, we played at various countryclubs. We played for a -- a guy named Mike Hall, a millionaire, in Texas -- parties for him and we played at this big hotel in Houston, can't think of the name of it now, it'll come to me, and the Mexican waiters didn't want to wait on us. And this man cursed the waiters out and told them if they wanted a job they'd better come on and wait on us, and so they served us right in the hotel dining room with his guests, only we had a different table.

We played at the Dallas -- I mean at the Houston Countryclub. For parties of -- I guess about 10 couples, people had been flown in from -- and that was something new then, from New York and different places, for this party, 10 or 12 couples. I remember, first time I'd ever seen this, a woman just walked up with her evening gown and jump in the pool, you know what I mean? It was quite exciting, you know, to see and play parties like this.
Uh-huh.

But this was back in the Roaring '20's, and we played dances in Houston, back in that day, Houston was cut up into wards, 5th Ward and 2nd Ward and the 3rd Ward. I forget the ward we played in, but it was closely -- it was pretty close to downtown Houston, and we would play dances there and we'd have to turn them away. The band was so popular back in those days.

Yes, we played all through that state, in 1928. We had Alphonso Trent, the owner of the band, hired another piano player, a boy named James Sherman, James Sherman joined us and made that tour with us out in -- in Texas. Sherman was the -- he only had nine fingers. He was originally from Philadelphia, and later years he played with the Charioteers. He was the pianist with the Charioteers.

Houston was -- was quite a city, for the band. We played several social affairs, black, at Houston. And the band was well thought of in the very best of circles. We also played out in West Texas, we -- I shall never forget the little town named Menard -- Menard, Texas. We opened up a new hotel out there. And that was rattlesnake country.

They booked us out there and they had no place for us to eat, so we had to eat in the basement of the hotel, We got paid -- we got paid for it, though, we got good money. But, that was back in the days when that was a time of the century that you'd like to forget about.

While in Dallas, Texas, I met a group of young musicians, one was named Bud Johnson, had a brother named Keg Johnson. Budd played tenor sax, Keg played trombone. A -- met an alto player named Booker Pitman. Booker Pitman was the grandson of the late Booker T. WASHINGTON. Booker Pitman I didn't see Booker Pitman for a year or two, until I ran into him out in Springfield, Mass. He was playing with the Blanche Calloway band. Shortly after that Booker Pitman left and went to Europe, he left Europe went to South America. He played every principal country in South America. The people in South America were crazy about him, especially in ARgentina.

AT one time in ARgentina, they had some kind of big affair and Booker Pitman was in Uruguay, I guess; he was in Montevideo, Uruguay, They came over and got him to lead that parade, He spoke Spanish, he spoke Portuguese, like the natives spoke it. He lived down in South America for 20 some years. I had the pleasure of flying down to Rio de Janeiro and I heard that Booker T. Pitman was playing at the It Club. And I happened to go by the It Club and Booker T. Pitman wasn't playing that day, but he was there with a group of people, about 12 or 14 people in a party, with the millionaire, George E. Ginley --
What year was this?
That was 1960. I'm just going from the time I met him in Texas --
Right.

Just sidetracking Texas for awhile, to -- to bring in Booker T. Pitman. I met Booker and we hugged each other because we hadn't seen each other in so many years. And Booker asked me to join them, they were going up to -- up to George E. Ginley's apartment. To hear some sounds, just like that. I said, okay. So we all got in cabs. And went up on the 25th floor at this penthouse of Mr. Ginley. And I found that Mr. Ginley knew more about jazz and American artists than I did. Because he had a blues room in his home, he had a symphony room in his home. And he had a jazz room. And he had records of Bessie Smith and all the great artists. He could talk about any form of music or any musician, or any -- any class of music you wanted to talk about, George E. Ginley could do it.

And I had a most beautiful evening, and a most beautiful stay in Rio, with Booker T. Pitman. I met his wife. She was a black woman, the color of my shoe, but a very smart person. And at this particular party there were people of color, from all over Brazil, business people. And they were all just like one big family. Mr. Ginley owned three or four magazines and he periodically would fly models in to appear in his magazines. So these ladies were flown out from California to appear in his magazines.
We had a beautiful morning -- evening and morning

there, discussing music and discussing jazz and what-not, Mr. Ginley also showed me a book that he had written on Zsa Zsa Gabor. She was one of his great friends, and I think she had been his guest there that same year.

Going into -- leaving Rio, we'll put that aside right now and we'll get back to -- get back to Texas. Trent's band went into San Antonio, Texas, we Played San Antonio. And I had a chance, my first time down there, to meet a fella named Troy Floyd, a bandleader. And in this particular band was a guy named -- played tenor sax, his name just slipped through mind just like -- just like that. Ah --
MR. : Hershel Evans.

MR. PILLARS: Hershel Evans. Hershel Evans, a very fine person a very fine tenor player. Hershel was born in Temple, Texas, and we discussed music and -- and the big bands and what-not. Later on Hershel left Texas and joined the Count Basie band, and made the original record the Count made of "One O'Clock Jump."

Also in Texas I had a chance to meet Don Albert, Don Albert was a bandleader there that's quite popular. With the Spanish people there. My brother, Charles Pillars, pined this particular band a year or two later. More about that later, too.
The band left San Antonio, --
MR. : Excuse me -- your brother joined the
No, he joined -- my brother joined the Don Albert band.
Oh, I see.
shortly after that, see.
I see.
That was before he joined the Alphonso Trent band.
Right.

We left San Antonio, we spent a few weeks -- a week or two in and out of San Antonio, and from there into Austin, where we played one-night stands, always to a large crowd because the band was popular back in that day, and from there we went into Ft. Worth, Teas. The band was real popular there, too. We would have had our regular dances, we had in each town our people leased out to promote the dances for us, put out placards, and that way we could realize more giving our own dances than to rely on people paying us a salary.

So at the end of 1928, 1929, comes along. The band moves back up into mid-America, and we do one-nighters and we play a few dates at the Greystone Ballroom, in Cincinnati, Ohio. We worked Wednesdays, Fridays, and Saturdays. And on -- no, Wednesday, Saturdays and Sundays. And that gave us a chance to book the band out on Friday, Thursdays and Fridays. And we kept that job until the Spring of the year 1929.

We were offered a job in Canada, Port On -- Port Stanley, Ontario, in Canada. We opened up in June, round the 1st of June. And was it cold? It was really cold up there. On a Saturday night we've have about, oh, I guess about 40 or 50 couples. But the owners were somehow or other they would pay us and we were there about four weeks before the weather started breaking. And the people started coming down there. But the owners of this particular ballroom realized that they weren't going to make it with our band as expensive as it was, so they were lucky enough to book us in Hamilton, Ontario at a little night spot there, where we went to work at 9:00 o'clock and off at 12:00 o'clock and the man would beg us not to play too much music.
And this would hurt us cause we liked to play.
What was the reason for that?

The man wanted to sell, you know, food and he wanted to sell, you know, drinks and things like that. And we were starting to playing and the place would be packed and jammed and people would get on the floor and dance. The longer we played, people stayed on the floor and danced. And he wouldn't sell anything. They'd beg us -- play three or four short tunes and then get off the bandstand and then get back up and play. Never had a job like that.
Right.
And the job was paying us a lot of money

back in those times, $50.00 a week. We worked on that job the whole -- the rest of the summer. '29. // -- and they booked us into the Palais Royale in Buffalo, New York, to open in September, 1929. Beautiful nightclub, we had to play a luncheon engagement, we had to play a dinner engagement, we'd come back at 10:00 o'clock at night and we'd play until 2:00 in the morning.

They furnished us our lunch, and they furnished us our dinner. The band was a riot, we had a beautiful band. And the band went over big. But the band didn't know anything about playing floorshows. So the owner hired a piano player who had worked in one of the theaters there, to be in charge of the floorshows and all we had to do then, was follow the piano player. And this we did.

I can't think of the piano player's name, but we worked on that job through October, and the union got together and decided that we shouldn't have that job, which was the best job in town. And they tricked us into meeting with the union officials, the international officials, and they told us what we should say, and they told us to put our scale down low, which we did, follow the union, and when the international came and interviewed us, they charged us with working under scale.
And they barred us from working that territory for two years. But we were lucky. We got a job at the Plantation
Club in Cleveland, Ohio.
Before you go to What were you doing in the Plantation Club? Why did the local union ask you to drop your -- your -- play below scale?
They wanted us to do that so that the international office would expel us --
Oh, I see.
It was a frameup.
All right, Okay.

It was a frameup. And we went to Cleveland, opened at the Club Plantation there, and we had become used to playing shows by that time, and they brought in a black show from New York City, a first class black show, brought Seamstress in, and chorus girls, had principals, and the producer of the show, his name was Earl Dancer, the husband of Ethel Waters.

And the show opened with a bang. We played dinner engagements and nightclub engagements, we used to work from 6:00 to 8:00, from 10:00 to 2:00. The band was a riot, the show was great. We played right on through 1929 into 1930. Two weeks after 1930, business started falling off. You know the crash came in 1929, and so it was gradually, the times were catching up with the crash. So in about another week and a half I used to go to work by streetcar, because streetcar would put me off a block from where I worked and I would get

on the streetcar in front of my house. So this particular day I went down to go to work, and I walked in and there had been a fire. And I saw my beautiful saxophone all curled up where it was burned up. All the instruments were burned up. So that meant that Trent's band were locked in Cleveland, Ohio without instruments. So, we were exploited by two or three groups, they gave benefit dances for us, and we --when the dance was all over, when you checked to see how much money you had in the pot, you had none. So there was a boy in town named Jenkins, I can't think of Jenkins' name, first name, last time I saw Jenkins he was in Providence Rhode Island. I got a gig, Jenkins got a gig for me, he couldn't make it and he loaned me his horn. I made that gig, I made $16.00 on that gig. I was so happy to get that money, I didn't know what to do.

And we stayed in Cleveland that whole winter. Finally Alphonso Trent's father got together and took us out to the King Factory in Cleveland, Ohio, and they bought everybody an instrument. His father, his people put up the money and got everybody in the band an instrument. Now Spring of 1930. We started a tour and we booked into Columbus, Ohio, and we get to Columbus, Ohio and there was another band booked in there, Sammy Stewart's orchestra and that was Sammy Stewart's home, he was a Chicago band, and his band was playing a homecoming there.

So both bands met at the Plaza Hotel there, which was a hotel out on Long Street in Columbus, Ohio. I remember that band, there was a young fella named Chu Berry, played tenor saxophone, playing with Sammy Stewart, and there was a guy named Big Sydney Catlett, drummer. Played drums. In our band, we had our original band, the dance we supposed to play very few people showed up, that meant that we were locked there, we were booked there in a pocket and we had to use some form of ingenuity in trying to get out.

I can remember that it was rough. A dollar was hard to come by during that time. Through some nook and crook, the brains of the band got together and we were able to move from there into Cincinnati, Ohio. And we hung around Cincinnati Ohio, for several weeks. Different guys in the band would get a job here or a job there. So we muffled and scuffled and scuffled and the people would just let us eat in the cafes and would let us owe them, they were good to us.

I was stopping at the Terry Hotel at that time, Mrs. Terry was very kind to me cause I always stayed with her. And everytime they ate, I ate, that meant everytime her family ate, I ate. Well during this time, the Mills Brothers started to becoming popular. I think they were broadcasting over radio station WLW. And, they became the rage around Cincinnati. We didn't do good around Cincinnati at all, so we finally booked the band and routed ourselves back south and back home.

And we scuffled and scuffled and scuffled and made our way down back into Texas. And I can remember a booking agent contacting us in Texas, and promised us a big job up in Syracuse, New York. We got together and saved what little money we could to get enough gasoline to get us back out East.

And the best we could do was just make enough to buy cigarettes and eat and buy gasoline. And so we scuffled and got ourselves together and we moved back east. Went through Little Rock, Arkansas, that's my home, I had a chance to see my people. Jeter had a chance to see his people. We hung around Little Rock several days, we played a little dance there, made a little money, and we moved on up -- we made it as far as Delaware, Ohio.

We couldn't go any farther. We had a guy in the band named Brent Sparks who contacted a fella who owned a filling station and this man was I believe a Mason. And this man came to the rescue of Brent Sparks and us, we got enough money to get into Cleveland, Ohio. We got back into Cleveland, Ohio and was able to borrow enough money to get us to Syracuse, New York. Jeter was driving a Model A Ford, three of us were riding with him. We had our instruments packed in the back in the rumble seat. The rumble seat could close down. And we pulled up in front of this place where we supposed to open, about 7:30 at night. And the place was plumb dark. There were weeds all around the place.

So we had been booked into a pocket. And there we were in Syracuse, New York, where no work, and that's when Stuff Smith left the band and went back to Buffalo, where his wife was. A. G. Godley Bartley left the band and went back to Cleveland, where his wife was. So the band almost broke up there in Syracuse, Peanuts Peter Holland stuck with the band, we had the reed section stuck with the band, Snub Mosley that Bosely stuck with the band, Crook, the banjo player, stuck with the band. So Jeter went out and he visited various places trying to secure some work formusicians and we got a job, one night playing in a roadhouse.

It was a four piece job, Jeter, myself, and the [Eugene] ed. banjo player, Crook, and we borrowed a drummer from somebody else. And we made $15.00 on that job. And that was the best $15.00 I ever made in my life.

We went back in and I took $5.00 of the dollars and kind of split it up with some of the guys in the band, We had a place where we could eat on credit, and so we got a few gigs that way, so finally the fellas who had booked us up there, in that pocket, picked us up and started booking us. And he took us all through upper New York state, Covered all the lakes, Lake Cuyahuga, the Finger Lakes, we played all through Pennsylvania and New York, and the best we could do is make two and a half and three hours a night, and the room it would cost us sometimes 50 and 75 cents, and we'd have
enough money to eat, and have enough money to buy cigarettes and go onto the next town.

1930 was a rough year. Yes, it was rough that year, so we regrouped, we finished that summer and regrouped back in Cincinnati, and we got the old band back together again. That's when Alphonso Trent hired Cy Oliver to write for the band. So we was offered a job in Cleveland, at the Hollywood Club, a nightclub, They knew about Trent's band, so we opened on a New Year's eve night.

They had two bands. I remember the Jack Teagarden was playing in the band, another Teagarden was playing trumpet Ray Bauduc was playing drums, and I can't think who was playing the reed section. The name of the band skips me right now, it'll come to be in a few minutes. That band -- that was one of the hottest bands, one of the greatest bands that I ever heard. And that band opened up New Year's eve night and we had to go on behind that band and we never -- I never sweated so hard in all my life. That was a great band, and they played real swing style.

That evening the band left and was paid off. The next night was New Year's night, the crowd was small. And just seemed like the crowds never did pick up. So after working there about -- about three and a half or four weeks, the club closed. So there we were, so we decided to leave Cleveland, and go West.

So we left and went on out to Oklahoma. We played a little ballroom in Oklahoma City, we played a ballroom in Tulsa, we played several dances in Tulsa and around Tulsa, and things just never -- never got better.

And we entered into 19-- that was 1931. Because we had opened in Cleveland New Year's eve, 1930, which through us into 1931. In 1931, we played Oklahoma, we played parts of Arkansas, which was Alphonso Trent's home, so that gave us the base, we could loaf there, lay off there, because Trent's people would take care of the band. We played dances in Little Rock, just couldn't make any money.

There -- it was a tough scuffle. Things was just rough. Everybody kept thinking it would be better next week or next month or the next few months, but it just kept getting worse and worse, so we finally realized that we were in the grip of a deep depression and that was it. By Oliver left the band. We went to Okmulgee, Oklahoma and we played around Holland Okmulgee awhile. Peanuts Van Lan became ill there and he was incoherent -- you could talk to him and nothing would happen and he couldn't understand you and the funniest thing that happened to him, I've never seen it happen before, he fell down a flight of steps and got up and said, 'What happened to me?' you know, and the guy had been incoherent for about 10 days, and so everybody was just so happy that he was -- he had come to, you know, I guess the shock had brought him around.

We played through Oklahoma, we even played church concerts. To no avail. And things were really tough. We played towns like Seminole. Many small towns. It was just rough. So we changed booking agents and I can't think of the booking agent we secured, but he decided to book us into Dallas and to play some dates at the countryclubs and what-not and this we did. So we left -- we had left Oklahoma and we had gone to Arkansas and played around through Missouri and different places and we went through Kansas City on our way back to Texas.

We played at a big countryclub in Dallas, Texas. I remember that. New Year's eve, 1931. We played Adolphus Hotel, for a big affair, but we never did get the money we were supposed to get. I don't know whether the booking agents were taking the money or what. But we never got what we were supposed to get, all we got was just a little hand-out, maybe $3.00 or $4.00. Four or five dollars a man.

So we strung up out through Texas, we hung around San Antonio, and also Austin, Texas. And, finally, we went out to Corpus Christi, Texas. You can't go no further than Corpus Christi, cause that's way out there on the Gulf. And the owners of two ballrooms in Tulsa, sent us a telegram, offering us a six-weeks engagement to come to Tulsa to play at this particular ballroom.
So we had to get some cab drivers to drive us to

Tulsa. We got to Tulsa and we got advanced money, that paid for the cab drivers so the cab drivers could go back to Corpus Christi. And we played this particular ballroom and the best we could make would be four and five dollars a night. And by the time you got through paying for your expenses, working about three nights a week, you didn't have much left. So we wound up in Oklahoma City at the Ritz Ballroom.

And we played about three or four nights a week there. And then I write to arranged with my brother Charles in Oklahoma City, who was playing with the Southern Serenaders, am I right? And we asked my brother Charles to join our band and that's when he joined our band. To the best of my knowledge, that was in 1932, am I right Charles? 1932.

We got telegrams from one or two booking agents. And everybody was happy about the whole thing. Many people talked about that show that we played. Many weeks and month later, friends from Cleveland, Ohio called up and wrote letters, telling us about the program. '42 -- the summer of '42 was good and kind to us.

In the meantime, we had been taking our band down to the Jefferson Barracks, playing for the troops about twice a month, free of charge. We would take the entire show and band down, and the troops seemed like they enjoyed it so much. And we enjoyed doing it. The latter part of 1942, we began losing

we'll keep coming." And I was able to fill in with various musicians here and there, to keep the band going. But those were the highlights of 1942.

1943, comes on the scene. We still had the same problem, trying to get musicians. It was a job, trying to get various ones who could play shows and fill the bill. So I took Otis and we went to the woodshed, meaning that we took various tunes, bar by bar, note by note, I found out -- when I first started playing music that that was the best way, if you couldn't do it any other way. And the first tune that I picked was Sweet Lorraine." And I worked with Otis

In the meantime, the Army was gradually taking fellows. But we stuck it out. And we stuck it out. In the meantime, my draft board called me in, and I had to go down to the Jefferson Barracks to be examined. I was examined and they passed me on through. When I got to the last post, I was talking to a captain and a major. And they asked me what did I think of the Army. I told them I thought the Army was a wonderful institution. I said, 'You gentlemen are doing your part, and I might as well do my part like you and everybody else.'

I told him, I said, 'To prove to you that I've tried to do my part, the night before last, I brought my band and my show down here to entertain all the troops down here, and I come down here -- been coming down here twice a month, for the last year.' And the major said, 'Was that your band?' I said, 'Yes, sir, major, that was our band.'

So they went in a huddle, and I was looking out the window. And they came back and told me, said, 'Pillars, I guess you'll still be leading the band.' I said, 'Okay,' and I went on downstairs, waiting for them to call me to go to the Army, and

I was the last one they called. And they said, 'Hayes Pillars, come upstairs, reject.' So I was rejected. And naturally -- I'm going to be honest -- I was happy, and glad that I didn't have to go.
And I went back home, I grabbed my little wife and hugged her, and I must say, that was a very happy day for me.

And you had -- he was a slow reader, and that -- he always was that. He never did improve too much on this. But once he got something, he had it, man, he could lead that section. He says, "We'll keep you in the States a few weeks, and then maybe we'll send you to Europe." I said, "It's a good deal." He says, "When can you join the band?" He says, "Okay, I'll tell you what I'll do. I'll book you, put you on the train, we'll get Pullmans for you, put you on the next morning, you'll get on the train, and you'll come on out to New York and we'll process you for USO." Sent us the contract and we signed it. We finished that night, Labor Day night, got on the train the next day, everybody had a lower berth except my wife and I. And I wanted it that way. wife and she wasn't feeling too well, and it would be hard for her to ride up -- to get up there in the berth. I said, "I'd appreciate it if you could get something better for me." And we arrived at New York, met Dick the next day, and he had us to meet him at the Nola Studio. I don't know if the Nola Studio is still active in New York or not, but this is a studio that's down on Broadway, about 54th and Broadway.
